The first: the answering of his supplication, and this is an honour (karama). The second: the giving him a child, and this is a strength (quwwa). The third: that he be singled out by his naming.

This indicates two matters. The first: his being specially chosen for it. The second: his being selected (istifa') by Him.

Muqatil said: He named him Yahya because he was a child between an aged father and an old mother.

﴿We have not made for him before a namesake﴾ (p-357). In it there are three sayings. The first: that is, no barren woman had borne one like him; this is said by Ibn Abbas. So the meaning would be: We have not made for him a like or an equal.

The second: that We did not make for Zakariya a child before Yahya; this is said by Mujahid.

The third: that before him no one had been named with his name; this is said by Qatada.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 8–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can I have a boy?﴾ That is, a child.

The second: because there is a sterility (ʿuqr) in her womb that corrupts the seed. He did not say this out of doubt after the revelation, but in the form of inquiry: "Will You make us return to youth, the two of us, or grant us a child when we are elderly?" ﴿And I have reached extreme old age (ʿitiyyan)﴾. The second: it is the wasting away of the bones, as said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: it is that which time has altered into dryness and desiccation, as said by Ibn ʿIsa. The poet said:

"Only the youth is excused, and one who has been ʿitiyyan in age is not excused."

Qatadah said: he was seventy-odd years old. Muqatil said: he was ninety-five years old.

Ibn ʿAbbas recited it as ʿisiyyan (with a different consonant), and it is thus in the codex of Ubayy, from their saying of an old man when he grows old: "qad ʿasa wa ʿataa" (he has become ʿasa and ʿataa). The meaning of both is one.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 12–15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength﴾. There are two opinions regarding who spoke these words. The first is that it is the saying of Zakariyya to Yahya when he grew up.

The second is the saying of God to Yahya when he reached maturity.

Regarding "the Book" in this verse, there are two opinions. The first is the scrolls of Ibrahim (Abraham).

The second is the Torah.

Regarding "with strength" (bi-quwwah), there are two interpretations. The first is with earnestness and striving, as said by Mujahid.

(p-360) The second is acting upon what it contains of commands and refraining from what it contains of prohibitions, as said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

﴿And We gave him judgment while still a child﴾. Regarding this, there are four interpretations. The first is understanding (lubb), as said by al-Hasan.

The second is comprehension (fahm), as said by Muqatil.

The third is rulings (al-ahkam) and knowledge of them.

The fourth is wisdom (hikmah).

The second: her house was eastward-facing, the place the sun shines upon. 'Atiyyah said this.

The third: a far-off, distant place. Qatadah said this.

The second: nine months. Abu al-Qasim al-Saymari related this to me.

The second: it was the name of a wicked man among the Children of Israel, well known for fornication, who was called "God-fearing." (p-365) The second: from her womb. This was said by some of the speakers of kalam, in Coptic.

﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first is that the sari (a stream, or a noble one) is her son 'Isa, because the sari is the exalted, the noble, derived from their saying: "So-and-so is among the sarawat (chieftains) of his people," meaning among their nobles. This was said by al-Hasan. According to this, 'Isa is the one who called to her from below her: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a sari﴾. The second: the sari is the river. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr,

(p-366) Qatadah and al-Dahhak, so that the palm tree would be food for her and the river would be drink for her. According to this, Jibril is the one who called to her: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a sari﴾. The third: it is an Arabic word derived from al-sirayah (flowing), so the sari was named because it flows in it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Easy of disposition, noble, possessing bounty, like a sari that the rivers feed."

It was also said that the name sari applies to what people cross of rivers by leaping.

Aban ibn Taghlib narrated in his Qur'an commentary a report from a number of unnamed transmitters: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Shaddad ibn Thumamah as a collector of zakat for the Banu Ka'b ibn Madhhij and wrote him a letter: (On what the irrigation channels, the streams, the water-wheels, the rivulets and the rain-fed lands water, a tenth; and half a tenth, at a just valuation, except for the lean and the stallion camels and what the grain-stalk raises from the ground. For every forty sheep, one sheep, except for the 'aqil, the akil and the rabi. From every thirty cows, a male or female calf, except for the barren, the nashit and the rashih. From every five camels that are mubawwalah, a musinnah of the sheep. There is no zakat on horses or on working camels. Witnessed by Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir al-Bajali and Shaddad ibn Thumamah, and written by al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.)"

Al-marasil are the springs; al-jadawil are the small rivers; al-nawahir are the water-wheels; al-dawafi' are the valleys; al-dawamir are the palms that do not bear fruit; al-lawaqih are the stallions; al-jafn is the vine; and what the grain-stalk raises from the ground is pardoned. The 'aqil is the ram of the sheep; the akil is the one raised for eating; the rabi is the one that raises its young; the 'aqir among cows is the one that does not conceive; the nashit is the stallion that moves from one land to another; and the rashih is the one that ploughs the land.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾, to the end of the verse.

There are four opinions concerning the palm tree:

(p-367) The first: it was a barniyyah (a type of date palm).

The second: it was sarfatah (a type of date palm), said by Abu Dawud.

The third: it was qarin.

The fourth: it was 'ajwah (a type of date), said by Mujahid.

Regarding "al-janiyy" (freshly picked) there are three opinions. The first: it is the ripe dates that are beginning to soften, said by Muqatil.

The second: the unripened dates that have not changed, said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

The third: that it is the fresh one with its dust.

It was also said that the palm tree had no top, and that it was winter, and Allah made it a sign.

Muqatil said: it turned green while she was looking; then it bore fruit while she was looking; then it ripened while she was looking.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So eat﴾, meaning from the fresh dates.

﴿And drink﴾, meaning from the sari.

﴿And let your eye be cooled﴾, meaning through the child. Regarding this there are three aspects. The first: "He came to cool your eye with joy," said by al-Asma'i, because the tear of joy is cool and the tear of sorrow is hot.

The second: "Be content of soul," said by al-Kalbi.

The third: "Your eye will be still"; for this reason it was said: there is nothing better for women who have just given birth than fresh dates and dates.

﴿And if you see any human﴾, meaning either to denounce you or to question you on her behalf.

﴿Then say: "Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast"﴾. There are two interpretations regarding this. The first: it means silence, and in some readings it has been recited: "li'l-Rahman samtan" (a vow of silence to the Most Merciful). This was the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and al-Dahhak.

The second: a fast from food, drink and speech, said by Qatadah.

(p-368) ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: she refrained from speaking so that her child would speak on her behalf, and thus her innocence would be established, said by Ibn Mas'ud, Wahb ibn Munabbih and Ibn Zayd.

The second: whoever fasted in that time did not speak to people, so she was permitted a measure of speech, said by al-Suddi.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-‘Uyun) on Surah 19, verses 27–33**

(p-369) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a monstrous thing﴾. On this there are five interpretations. The first: it is the ugliest kind of fabrication. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The second: it is a strange deed. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The third: it is a great matter. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The fourth: it is that which is feigned, derived from *al-fiyah*, which is lying. This is the view of al-Yazidi.

The fifth: it is falsehood.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O sister of Harun﴾. Regarding the man to whom she was attributed, there are four opinions. The first: he was a righteous man among the Children of Israel, and whoever was known for righteousness was attributed to him. This is the view of Mujahid and Ka‘b, and al-Mughirah ibn Shu‘bah traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second: he was Harun, the brother of Musa, and she was attributed to him because she was among his descendants, just as one says "O brother of the sons of so-and-so." This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: he was her full brother, from both her father and her mother. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The fourth: he was a wicked man who openly displayed wickedness, and she was attributed to him. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

﴿Your mother was not a *baghiyy*﴾, that is, an adulteress.

The adulteress was called *baghiyy* because she seeks (*tabghi*) fornication, that is, she seeks it out.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So she pointed to him﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: she pointed to God, but they did not understand her gesture. This is the view of ‘Ata’.

The second, and this is the more apparent: she pointed to ‘Isa. This was either by revelation from God to her, or because of her confidence in herself that God, the Exalted, would manifest her innocence. So she pointed to him, meaning: speak to him. This allows two possibilities. The first: she referred the answer to him, seeking to be sufficed by him. The second: she turned to him so that his speech on her behalf would serve as proof of her innocence.

﴿They said: "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle?"﴾ Regarding *kana* ("is") in this place, there are two possibilities. The first: it means "will be," so the meaning is: "one who will be a child in the cradle." This is the view of Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: it is an extra connecting particle (*silah*, a particle that links a clause without adding meaning), and the meaning is "one who is in the cradle." This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding *al-mahd* ("the cradle"), there are two possibilities. The first: it is the child's familiar bed for sleeping.

(p-370) The second: it is her lap, in which she nurses him. This is the view of Qatadah.

It is said that they became angry and said: "Her mockery of us is greater than her fornication." This is the view of al-Suddi.

When he spoke, they said: "Indeed, this is a great matter."

﴿He said: "Indeed I am the servant of God"﴾. He placed his affirmation of servanthood first in order to refute the claim of those who attributed lordship (*ruboobiyyah*) to him. It was God who made him speak this, because He knew what the exaggerators would say about him.

﴿He has given me the Book﴾, that is, He will give me the Book.

﴿And made me a prophet﴾. Regarding this there are two possibilities. The first: "and He will make me a prophet," and the speech in the cradle is among the preliminaries of his prophethood.

The second: he was, at the time of his speaking to them in the cradle, a prophet with full intellect, and for this reason this miracle was granted to him. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Surely I will stone you﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: with stones, until you keep away from me. This is related from al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verse 49–50:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We bestowed upon them a tongue of truthfulness, elevated﴾. In this there are two interpretations.

The first: We bestowed upon them a good remembrance and a fine praise. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, and that is because the gathering of the community (al-milk, here understood as the people or the community of believers) is by the goodness of the praise bestowed upon it.

It may also be understood as a third saying: that it means fulfilling promises and covenants.

(p-376) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the Mount﴾. Al-Tur is a mountain in al-Sham (Syria); Allah called him from its right side.

In this there are two interpretations. The first: from the right of Musa (Moses). The second: from the right of the mountain; this is what Muqatil said.

﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. In this there are three interpretations. The first: He brought him near to the place which He honored and exalted by letting him hear His speech.

The second: He brought him near to the highest of the veils, until he heard the scratching of the pen. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said, and others said: until he heard the scratching of the pen with which the Torah was written.

The third: He brought him near in a manner of honor and selection, not a manner of drawing close and bringing nearer, because He is not described as dwelling in one place rather than another, so that He would come near from a distance or move away from nearness. This is what Ibn Bahr said.

Regarding His saying: ﴿najiyyan (as a confidant)﴾, there are three interpretations. The first: it is derived from najwa (secret conversation), and secret conversation occurs only in privacy; this is what Qutrub said.

The second: He saved him (najjahu) because of his truthfulness; it is derived from najah (salvation).

The third: He elevated him after bringing him near; it is derived from najwa, which means elevation. Al-Hasan said: Musa did not receive anything of the speech with which He conversed with him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 54–55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mention in the Book Ishmael; indeed he was true to his promise﴾. He described him as true to his promise because he promised a man that he would wait for him. Ibn ʿAbbas said: a year, until the man came to him.

Yazid al-Raqqashi said: he waited for him twenty-two days.

Muqatil said: he waited for him three days.

(p-377) ﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: he enjoined his people, and called them his family. The second: he began with his family before his people.

As for prayer and zakat, what we have already mentioned applies.

According to the view of the majority, he is Ishmael son of Abraham.

Some exegetes claimed that he is not Ishmael son of Abraham, because Ishmael died before Abraham. They said this is Ishmael son of Ezekiel, whom God sent to his people, and they flayed the skin of his head. So God gave him the choice regarding whatever punishment he wished to inflict on them, and he asked Him to pardon them, was content with His reward, and entrusted their affair to Him, whether to pardon them or to punish them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 56–57:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: that Idris (Idris) was raised up to the fourth heaven. This is the view of Anas ibn Malik in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ka'b, and Mujahid.

The second: that He raised him to the sixth heaven. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, and he is raised up in the heaven.

They differed concerning his death there, on two views. The first: that he died there. This was said by Muqatil, and it was said that he died between the fourth and fifth heavens.

The second: that he is alive there and did not die, like 'Isa (Jesus).

Ibn Ishaq narrated that Idris was the first of the children of Adam to be given prophethood, and the first to write with the pen, and he isUkhnukh ibn Yard ibn Mihla'il ibn Qaynan ibn Anush ibn Shith ibn Adam.

Ibn al-Azhar related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Idris was the first to take up weapons and fight in the path of Allah and take captives, and the first to wear clothing, whereas people had previously worn hides; and the first to establish weights and measures, and he established the science of the stars. And Allah knows best.

Allah says: ﴿They fell down prostrating and weeping﴾. That is, prostrating to Allah, and "bukiyyan" is the plural of "baki" (weeping ones), so that the prostration is out of hope (raghbah) and the weeping out of awe (rahbah).

It has been narrated in a hadith: "This is the prostration, so where is the weeping?" That is, "This is the hope (raghbah), so where is the awe (rahbah)?" Because worship is not made sincere except through both hope and awe.

(p-٣٧٩) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then there succeeded them a later generation﴾, and the rest of the verse.

Regarding the difference between *khalf* (with a sukun on the lam) and *khalaf* (with a fatha on the lam), there are two views. The first is that it is with the fatha when the one who succeeds is of the same people, and with the sukun when the one who succeeds is not of the same people. The second is that *khalf* with the sukun is used in dispraise, and *khalaf* with the fatha is used in praise. Labid said:

> Gone are those among whose flanks one lived,
> and I remain in a *khalf* like the mangy hide.

Regarding this *khalf*, there are two opinions. The first is that they are the Jews, after the prophets who had preceded them. This was said by Muqatil.

The second is that they are among the Muslims.

Based on this, regarding His saying ﴿after them﴾, there are two views. The first is: after the Prophet (ﷺ), from the era of the Companions until the Hour arrives, as al-Walid ibn Qays transmitted, which Ibrahim related from Ubayda.

The second is: that they come after the era of the Companions.

Al-Walid ibn Qays narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "After sixty years there will come a *khalf* who neglected the prayer."

and the rest of the verse.

Regarding their neglecting the prayer, there are two views. The first is delaying it beyond its times, as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz.

The second is abandoning it, as said by al-Qurazi.

A third possibility is that their neglect of it is failing to fulfill its conditions.

(p-٣٨٠) ﴿So they will meet with *ghayy*﴾. Regarding it there are five sayings. The first: it is a valley in Hell, as said by Aisha and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: it is loss, as said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: it is evil, as said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: it is straying away from Paradise.

The fifth: it is failure, and from this is the poet's saying:

> Whoever meets good, people praise his affair,
> and whoever goes astray (*yaghwa*) will not lack one who blames him for his error.

"Whoever *yaghwa*" means: whoever *yakhib* (fails and loses).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 61–63:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾ has two interpretations. The first: corrupt speech (al-kalam al-fasid). The second: falsehood (al-khulf), as said by Muqatil.

﴿Except the word "Peace"﴾ has two interpretations:

(p-381) The first: except safety (al-salamah).

The second: the greeting of the angels to them, as said by Muqatil.

﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾ has two interpretations. The first: the Arabs, when they had their morning meal (al-ghada') and evening meal (al-'asha'), were content, so God informed them that they would have a morning meal and an evening meal in Paradise, even though there is no night or day in Paradise.

The second: its meaning is the measure of the morning (al-bukrah) and the measure of the evening (al-'ashiyy) of the days of this world, as said by Ibn Jurayj.

It is also said that they know the measure of the night by the lowering of the veils and the closing of the doors, and the measure of the day by the raising of the veils and the opening of the doors.

It is possible that the morning (al-bukrah) is before they busy themselves with their pleasures, and the evening (al-'ashiyy) is after they finish their pleasures, because between them there occur intervals of transition from one state to another.

On the words of Allah, ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾, there are two opinions.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verse 71–72:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: it means the fever and sickness. This is the view of Mujahid.

Abu Hurayrah narrated, saying: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to visit a man among his companions who had a fever, and I was with him. The Messenger of Allah said: '(Be glad, for Allah, exalted and majestic, says: It is My fire. I impose it upon My believing servant so that it may be his portion of the Fire).'" That is, in the Hereafter.

The second: it means Jahannam (Hell).

Then concerning this there are two opinions. The first: it means that the disbelievers pass through it, not the believer. This is the view of Ikrimah, and his saying ﴿and there is none of you﴾ means "none of them," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their Lord gave them to drink a pure drink﴾, then He said: ﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward﴾, meaning, for them.

The second: that it intends both the believer and the disbeliever.

Ibn Zayd narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "(The slippers and the slipping women on that day are many)." Concerning the manner of their passing through it there are two opinions:

(p-385) The first: entering into it.

Ibn Abbas said: "Every righteous and wicked person will certainly pass through it. However, it touches the wicked and not the righteous."

He said: The supplication of those who passed on was: "O Allah, bring me out of the Fire safe, and admit me into Paradise with knowledge."

The second opinion: the passing of the Muslim over it is arriving at it while looking at it and rejoicing at being saved from it. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], meaning he reached it.

And like the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:

"When they came to the water, its pools blue, they set down the staves of the settled, encamped one."

It may bear a third opinion: that what is meant by this passing is the passing of the Standing of the Resurrection, which gathers every righteous and wicked person.

﴿It was upon your Lord a decree decided﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: a required decree, this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: an obligatory oath, this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 73–74:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station﴾. In this there are two views. The first: a place of residence in Paradise or in the Fire.

The second: it means a speech established upon dispute and argument, that is: which of them has a proof that prevails through obedience, and which of them has a proof that is refuted through disobedience? The evidence for this is the verse of Labid:

"And a tight station, whose opening was made by my tongue, my sword and my argument."

﴿And better in assembly﴾. In this there are two views. The first: better in gathering (majlis).

The second: wider in livelihood.

It may also bear a third meaning: which of the two is better in station at the place of gathering (on the Day of Reckoning), the one for whom reward or punishment is decreed? ﴿And better in assembly﴾: a place of residence in Paradise or in the Fire. Tha'lab said: al-maqam with a dammah on the meem means residence, and with a fathah on it means assembly (majlis).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Furnishings and appearance﴾. In this there are four views. The first: that al-athath means property, and al-riy' means outward appearance; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The poet said:

"Did the howdahs part, the day they departed, with what is beautiful in appearance from the furnishings?"

The second: that al-athath is what is new of the household garments, and al-riy' is being well-watered with blessing.

The third: al-athath is what people do not see, and al-riy' is what people see.

The fourth: its meaning is greater wealth and finer forms.

It may also bear a fifth meaning: that al-athath is what is prepared for use, and al-riy' is what is prepared for beauty.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 77–80:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs﴾. Scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, on two views. First: it concerns al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi; this was said by Jabir, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

Second: it concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; this was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And [he says], "I will be given wealth and children"﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-waladan﴾ with a damma on the waw, while the rest read it with a fatha. The difference in pronouncing it with a damma or a fatha is explained on two views. First: the two are dialect forms with the same meaning, as one says walad and wuld, and 'adam and 'udm. al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

Indeed I have seen people who multiplied wealth and offspring (wuldan).

Second: the tribe of Qays uses wuld with a damma as a collective noun, and walad with a fatha as a singular.

Regarding His saying, ﴿"I will surely be given wealth and children"﴾, there are two views. First: he meant in the Garden, mockingly, concerning what God promised for obedience and worship; this was said by al-Kalbi. Second: he meant in this world, and this is the view of the majority.

Regarding it there are two possible views: First: "If I remain upon the religion of my forefathers and the worship of my gods, I will surely be given wealth and children." Second: the meaning is, "Had I been upon falsehood, I would not have been given wealth and children."

﴿Has he looked into the unseen﴾ may bear two meanings: First: the meaning is, "Has he known the unseen, that He will give him wealth and children despite his disbelief?" Second: "Has he known the unseen, for what God has given him despite his disbelief?"

﴿Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾. Regarding it there are two views: First: it means a righteous deed he has sent ahead; this was said by Qatada. Second: a word God has pledged to him; this was related by Ibn 'Isa.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾. Regarding it there are two views: First: God will strip him of the wealth and children He gave him in this world. Second: He will deprive him of what he wished for in the Hereafter of wealth and children.

﴿And he will come to Us alone﴾. Regarding it there are two views: First: without wealth and without children. Second: without any helper or supporter.

(p-389) His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They will deny their worship of them﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

First: they will deny that they had worshipped them, because of what they witnessed of its evil consequence.

Second: they will disbelieve in those they worshipped and will call them liars.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And they will be against them as opponents﴾. Concerning this there are five opinions:

First: they will be helpers in their disputes against them; this is said by Mujahid.

Second: they will be companions in the Fire who curse them; this is said by Qatadah.

Third: they will be enemies to them; this is said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: they will be a calamity upon them; this is said by Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: that they will be lied about in contrast to what they had estimated concerning them and hoped from them; this is said by Ibn Bahr.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do you not see that We send the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: they agitate them with agitation until they bring them into sins; this is said by Qatadah.

Second: they lead them astray with misguidance; this is said by al-Dahhak.

Third: they urge them on to evil with urging: "Go on, go on with this matter until they bring them into the Fire"; this is said by Ibn Abbas.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So do not be hasty against them. We are only counting out their days for them, a counting﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: We count their deeds with a count; this is said by Qutrub.

Second: We count the days of their lives; this is said by al-Kalbi.

Third: We count the period of their respite until the time of retribution against them by the sword and jihad; this is said by Muqatil.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 19, verses 96–98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾, concerning which there are two views:

(p-391) One: love in the world among the righteous, and awe in the hearts of the wicked.

The second: Allah loves them and the people love them. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: When Allah loves a servant, He places love for him in the hearts of the people of the heavens, then He places it in the hearts of the people of the earth.

It may also bear a third meaning: that He will grant them a good reputation.

Ka'b said: A servant's praise does not settle in the world until it settles among the people of the heavens.

al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that He placed affection for him in the hearts of the believers.

His saying, may He be mighty and majestic: ﴿a people of contention﴾, concerning which there are three interpretations: One: sinners, as said by Mujahid.

The second: people who persist intensely in disputation, derived from *al-ladud* (the side of the mouth, i.e., "that which is poured into the mouth as medicine"), so their persistence in disputation with their mouths is like the pouring of medicine into the mouths. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The poet said:

They oppressed me with their fury against me, as if the enmity in their breasts were boiling in a cauldron.

The third: contentious argument in falsehood, as said by Qatadah, derived from *al-ladud*, which means one who is extremely contentious.

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Yet he is the most contentious of opponents﴾ [2:204]. And the poet said:

I pass the night, confiding to my worries, as if I am disputing with people who are fierce in argument.

His saying, may He be mighty and majestic: ﴿a faint sound﴾, concerning which there are three sayings: One: a sound, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second: a sensation (perceptible sound or movement), as said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that it is what is not understood from a sound or a movement, as said by al-Yazidi.
